## `createServer`

**Type Signature:**

```ts
async function createServer(inlineConfig?: InlineConfig): Promise<ViteDevServer>
```

**Example Usage:**

```ts twoslash
import { createServer } from 'vite'

const server = await createServer({
  // any valid user config options, plus `mode` and `configFile`
  configFile: false,
  root: import.meta.dirname,
  server: {
    port: 1337,
  },
})
await server.listen()

server.printUrls()
server.bindCLIShortcuts({ print: true })
```

::: tip NOTE
When using `createServer` and `build` in the same Node.js process, both functions rely on `process.env.NODE_ENV` to work properly, which also depends on the `mode` config option. To prevent conflicting behavior, set `process.env.NODE_ENV` or the `mode` of the two APIs to `development`. Otherwise, you can spawn a child process to run the APIs separately.
:::

::: tip NOTE
When using [middleware mode](/config/server-options.html#server-middlewaremode) combined with [proxy config for WebSocket](/config/server-options.html#server-proxy), the parent http server should be provided in `middlewareMode` to bind the proxy correctly.

<details>
<summary>Example</summary>

```ts twoslash

import { createServer } from 'vite'

const parentServer = http.createServer() // or express, koa, etc.

const vite = await createServer({
  server: {
    // Enable middleware mode
    middlewareMode: {
      // Provide the parent http server for proxy WebSocket
      server: parentServer,
    },
    proxy: {
      '/ws': {
        target: 'ws://localhost:3000',
        // Proxying WebSocket
        ws: true,
      },
    },
  },
})

// @noErrors: 2339
parentServer.use(vite.middlewares)
```

</details>

## `InlineConfig`

The `InlineConfig` interface extends `UserConfig` with additional properties:

- `configFile`: specify config file to use. If not set, Vite will try to automatically resolve one from project root. Set to `false` to disable auto resolving.

## `ResolvedConfig`

The `ResolvedConfig` interface has all the same properties of a `UserConfig`, except most properties are resolved and non-undefined. It also contains utilities like:

- `config.assetsInclude`: A function to check if an `id` is considered an asset.
- `config.logger`: Vite's internal logger object.

```ts

   * The resolved Vite config object.
   */
  config: ResolvedConfig
  /**
   * A connect app instance

   * - Can also be used as the handler function of a custom http server
   *   or as a middleware in any connect-style Node.js frameworks.
   *
   * https://github.com/senchalabs/connect#use-middleware
   */
  middlewares: Connect.Server
  /**
   * Native Node http server instance.
   * Will be null in middleware mode.
   */
  httpServer: http.Server | null
  /**
   * Chokidar watcher instance. If `config.server.watch` is set to `null`,
   * it will not watch any files and calling `add` or `unwatch` will have no effect.

   */
  watcher: FSWatcher
  /**
   * WebSocket server with `send(payload)` method.
   */
  ws: WebSocketServer
  /**
   * Rollup plugin container that can run plugin hooks on a given file.
   */
  pluginContainer: PluginContainer
  /**
   * Module graph that tracks the import relationships, url to file mapping
   * and hmr state.
   */
  moduleGraph: ModuleGraph
  /**
   * The resolved urls Vite prints on the CLI (URL-encoded). Returns `null`
   * in middleware mode or if the server is not listening on any port.
   */
  resolvedUrls: ResolvedServerUrls | null
  /**
   * Programmatically resolve, load and transform a URL and get the result
   * without going through the http request pipeline.
   */
  transformRequest(
    url: string,
    options?: TransformOptions,
  ): Promise<TransformResult | null>
  /**
   * Apply Vite built-in HTML transforms and any plugin HTML transforms.
   */
  transformIndexHtml(
    url: string,
    html: string,
    originalUrl?: string,
  ): Promise<string>
  /**
   * Load a given URL as an instantiated module for SSR.
   */
  ssrLoadModule(
    url: string,
    options?: { fixStacktrace?: boolean },
  ): Promise<Record<string, any>>
  /**
   * Fix ssr error stacktrace.
   */
  ssrFixStacktrace(e: Error): void
  /**
   * Triggers HMR for a module in the module graph. You can use the `server.moduleGraph`
   * API to retrieve the module to be reloaded. If `hmr` is false, this is a no-op.
   */
  reloadModule(module: ModuleNode): Promise<void>
  /**
   * Start the server.
   */
  listen(port?: number, isRestart?: boolean): Promise<ViteDevServer>
  /**
   * Restart the server.
   *
   * @param forceOptimize - force the optimizer to re-bundle, same as --force cli flag
   */
  restart(forceOptimize?: boolean): Promise<void>
  /**
   * Stop the server.
   */
  close(): Promise<void>
  /**
   * Bind CLI shortcuts
   */
  bindCLIShortcuts(options?: BindCLIShortcutsOptions<ViteDevServer>): void
  /**
   * Calling `await server.waitForRequestsIdle(id)` will wait until all static imports
   * are processed. If called from a load or transform plugin hook, the id needs to be
   * passed as a parameter to avoid deadlocks. Calling this function after the first
   * static imports section of the module graph has been processed will resolve immediately.
   * @experimental

  waitForRequestsIdle: (ignoredId?: string) => Promise<void>

```

:::info
`waitForRequestsIdle` is meant to be used as an escape hatch to improve DX for features that can't be implemented following the on-demand nature of the Vite dev server. It can be used during startup by tools like Tailwind to delay generating the app CSS classes until the app code has been seen, avoiding flashes of style changes. When this function is used in a load or transform hook, and the default HTTP1 server is used, one of the six http channels will be blocked until the server processes all static imports. Vite's dependency optimizer currently uses this function to avoid full-page reloads on missing dependencies by delaying loading of pre-bundled dependencies until all imported dependencies have been collected from static imported sources. Vite may switch to a different strategy in a future major release, setting `optimizeDeps.holdUntilCrawlEnd: false` by default to avoid the performance hit in large applications during cold start.
:::

# Plugin API

Vite plugins extends Rolldown's plugin interface with a few extra Vite-specific options. As a result, you can write a Vite plugin once and have it work for both dev and build.

**It is recommended to go through [Rolldown's plugin documentation](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api) first before reading the sections below.**

## Authoring a Plugin

Vite strives to offer established patterns out of the box, so before creating a new plugin make sure that you check the [Features guide](/guide/features) to see if your need is covered. Also review available community plugins, both in the form of a [compatible Rollup plugin](https://github.com/rollup/awesome) and [Vite Specific plugins](https://github.com/vitejs/awesome-vite#plugins).

When creating a plugin, you can inline it in your `vite.config.js`. There is no need to create a new package for it. Once you see that a plugin was useful in your projects, consider sharing it to help others [in the ecosystem](https://chat.vite.dev).

::: tip
When learning, debugging, or authoring plugins, we suggest including [vite-plugin-inspect](https://github.com/antfu/vite-plugin-inspect) in your project. It allows you to inspect the intermediate state of Vite plugins. After installing, you can visit `localhost:5173/__inspect/` to inspect the modules and transformation stack of your project. Check out install instructions in the [vite-plugin-inspect docs](https://github.com/antfu/vite-plugin-inspect).
![vite-plugin-inspect](../images/vite-plugin-inspect.webp)
:::

## Conventions

If the plugin doesn't use Vite specific hooks and can be implemented as a [Compatible Rolldown Plugin](#rolldown-plugin-compatibility), then it is recommended to use the [Rolldown Plugin naming conventions](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api#conventions).

- Rolldown Plugins should have a clear name with `rolldown-plugin-` prefix.
- Include `rolldown-plugin` and `vite-plugin` keywords in package.json `keywords` field.

This exposes the plugin to be also used in pure Rolldown or Rollup based projects.

For Vite only plugins

- Vite Plugins should have a clear name with `vite-plugin-` prefix.
- Include `vite-plugin` keyword in package.json `keywords` field.
- Include a section in the plugin docs detailing why it is a Vite only plugin (for example, it uses Vite specific plugin hooks).

If your plugin is only going to work for a particular framework, its name should be included as part of the prefix.

- `vite-plugin-vue-` prefix for Vue Plugins
- `vite-plugin-react-` prefix for React Plugins
- `vite-plugin-svelte-` prefix for Svelte Plugins

See also [Virtual Modules Convention](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api#virtual-modules).

## Plugins Config

Users will add plugins to the project `devDependencies` and configure them using the `plugins` array option.

```js [vite.config.js]
import vitePlugin from 'vite-plugin-feature'
import rollupPlugin from 'rollup-plugin-feature'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [vitePlugin(), rollupPlugin()],
})
```

Falsy plugins will be ignored, which can be used to easily activate or deactivate plugins.

`plugins` also accepts presets including several plugins as a single element. This is useful for complex features (like framework integration) that are implemented using several plugins. The array will be flattened internally.

```js
// framework-plugin
import frameworkRefresh from 'vite-plugin-framework-refresh'
import frameworkDevtools from 'vite-plugin-framework-devtools'

export default function framework(config) {
  return [frameworkRefresh(config), frameworkDevTools(config)]
}
```

```js [vite.config.js]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import framework from 'vite-plugin-framework'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [framework()],
})
```

## Simple Examples

:::tip
It is common convention to author a Vite/Rolldown/Rollup plugin as a factory function that returns the actual plugin object. The function can accept options which allows users to customize the behavior of the plugin.
:::

### Transforming Custom File Types

```js
const fileRegex = /\.(my-file-ext)$/

export default function myPlugin() {
  return {
    name: 'transform-file',

    transform: {
      filter: {
        id: fileRegex,
      },
      handler(src, id) {
        return {
          code: compileFileToJS(src),
          map: null, // provide source map if available
        }
      },
    },
  }
}
```

### Importing a Virtual File

Virtual modules allow you to pass build time information to the source files using normal ESM import syntax. See [Virtual Modules Convention](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api#virtual-modules) for the full convention.

```js
import { exactRegex } from '@rolldown/pluginutils'

export default function myPlugin() {
  const virtualModuleId = 'virtual:my-module'
  const resolvedVirtualModuleId = '\0' + virtualModuleId

  return {
    name: 'my-plugin', // required, will show up in warnings and errors
    resolveId: {
      filter: { id: exactRegex(virtualModuleId) },
      handler() {
        return resolvedVirtualModuleId
      },
    },
    load: {
      filter: { id: exactRegex(resolvedVirtualModuleId) },
      handler() {
        return `export const msg = "from virtual module"`
      },
    },
  }
}
```

Which allows importing the module in JavaScript:

```js
import { msg } from 'virtual:my-module'

console.log(msg)
```

In Vite, since `\0` is not a permitted char in import URLs, a `\0{id}` virtual id ends up encoded as `/@id/__x00__{id}` during dev in the browser. The id is decoded back before entering the plugins pipeline, so this is not seen by plugin hooks code.

## Rolldown Hooks

During dev, the Vite dev server creates a plugin container that invokes [Rolldown Build Hooks](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api#build-hooks) the same way Rolldown does it.

All rolldown hooks are [per-environment hooks](/guide/api-environment-plugins#per-environment-hooks-and-global-hooks).

The following hooks are called once on server start:

- [`options`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#options)
- [`buildStart`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#buildstart)

The following hooks are called on each incoming module request:

- [`resolveId`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#resolveid)
- [`load`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#load)
- [`transform`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#transform)

These hooks also have an extended `options` parameter with additional Vite-specific properties. You can read more in the [SSR documentation](/guide/ssr#ssr-specific-plugin-logic).

Some `resolveId` calls' `importer` value may be an absolute path for a generic `index.html` at root as it's not always possible to derive the actual importer due to Vite's unbundled dev server pattern. For imports handled within Vite's resolve pipeline, the importer can be tracked during the import analysis phase, providing the correct `importer` value.

The following hooks are called when the server is closed:

- [`buildEnd`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#buildend)
- [`closeBundle`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#closebundle)

Note that the [`moduleParsed`](https://rolldown.rs/reference/Interface.Plugin#moduleparsed) hook is **not** called during dev, because Vite avoids full AST parses for better performance.

[Output Generation Hooks](https://rolldown.rs/apis/plugin-api#output-generation-hooks) (except `closeBundle`) are **not** called during dev.

# Static Asset Handling

- Related: [Public Base Path](./build#public-base-path)
- Related: [`assetsInclude` config option](/config/shared-options.md#assetsinclude)

## Importing Asset as URL

Importing a static asset will return the resolved public URL when it is served:

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
import imgUrl from './img.png'
document.getElementById('hero-img').src = imgUrl
```

For example, `imgUrl` will be `/src/img.png` during development, and become `/assets/img.2d8efhg.png` in the production build.

The behavior is similar to webpack's `file-loader`. The difference is that the import can be either using absolute public paths (based on project root during dev) or relative paths.

- `url()` references in CSS are handled the same way.

- If using the Vue plugin, asset references in Vue SFC templates are automatically converted into imports.

- Common image, media, and font filetypes are detected as assets automatically. You can extend the internal list using the [`assetsInclude` option](/config/shared-options.md#assetsinclude).

- Referenced assets are included as part of the build assets graph, will get hashed file names, and can be processed by plugins for optimization.

- Assets smaller in bytes than the [`assetsInlineLimit` option](/config/build-options.md#build-assetsinlinelimit) will be inlined as base64 data URLs.

- Git LFS placeholders are automatically excluded from inlining because they do not contain the content of the file they represent. To get inlining, make sure to download the file contents via Git LFS before building.

- TypeScript, by default, does not recognize static asset imports as valid modules. To fix this, include [`vite/client`](./features#client-types).

::: tip Inlining SVGs through `url()`
When passing a URL of SVG to a manually constructed `url()` by JS, the variable should be wrapped within double quotes.

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
import imgUrl from './img.svg'
document.getElementById('hero-img').style.background = `url("${imgUrl}")`
```

:::

### Explicit URL Imports

Assets that are not included in the internal list or in `assetsInclude` can be explicitly imported as a URL using the `?url` suffix. This is useful, for example, to import [Houdini Paint Worklets](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/CSS/paintWorklet_static).

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
import workletURL from 'extra-scalloped-border/worklet.js?url'
CSS.paintWorklet.addModule(workletURL)
```

### Explicit Inline Handling

Assets can be explicitly imported with inlining or no inlining using the `?inline` or `?no-inline` suffix respectively.

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
import imgUrl1 from './img.svg?no-inline'
import imgUrl2 from './img.png?inline'
```

### Importing Asset as String

Assets can be imported as strings using the `?raw` suffix.

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
import shaderString from './shader.glsl?raw'
```

### Importing Script as a Worker

Scripts can be imported as web workers with the `?worker` or `?sharedworker` suffix.

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
// Separate chunk in the production build
import Worker from './shader.js?worker'
const worker = new Worker()
```

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
// sharedworker
import SharedWorker from './shader.js?sharedworker'
const sharedWorker = new SharedWorker()
```

```js twoslash
import 'vite/client'
// ---cut---
// Inlined as base64 strings
import InlineWorker from './shader.js?worker&inline'
```

Check out the [Web Worker section](./features.md#web-workers) for more details.

## The `public` Directory

If you have assets that are:

- Never referenced in source code (e.g. `robots.txt`)
- Must retain the exact same file name (without hashing)
- ...or you simply don't want to have to import an asset first just to get its URL

Then you can place the asset in a special `public` directory under your project root. Assets in this directory will be served at root path `/` during dev, and copied to the root of the dist directory as-is.

The directory defaults to `<root>/public`, but can be configured via the [`publicDir` option](/config/shared-options.md#publicdir).

Note that you should always reference `public` assets using root absolute path - for example, `public/icon.png` should be referenced in source code as `/icon.png`.

::: tip Choosing between imports and the `public` directory

In general, prefer **importing assets** unless you specifically need the guarantees provided by the `public` directory.

:::

## new URL(url, import.meta.url)

[import.meta.url](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/import.meta) is a native ESM feature that exposes the current module's URL. Combining it with the native [URL constructor](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URL), we can obtain the full, resolved URL of a static asset using relative path from a JavaScript module:

```js
const imgUrl = new URL('./img.png', import.meta.url).href

document.getElementById('hero-img').src = imgUrl
```

This works natively in modern browsers - in fact, Vite doesn't need to process this code at all during development!

This pattern also supports dynamic URLs via template literals:

```js
function getImageUrl(name) {
  // note that this does not include files in subdirectories
  return new URL(`./dir/${name}.png`, import.meta.url).href
}
```

During the production build, Vite will perform necessary transforms so that the URLs still point to the correct location even after bundling and asset hashing. However, the URL string must be static so it can be analyzed, otherwise the code will be left as is, which can cause runtime errors if `build.target` does not support `import.meta.url`.

```js
// Vite will not transform this
const imgUrl = new URL(imagePath, import.meta.url).href
```

::: details How it works

Vite will transform the `getImageUrl` function to:

```js
import __img0png from './dir/img0.png'
import __img1png from './dir/img1.png'

function getImageUrl(name) {
  const modules = {
    './dir/img0.png': __img0png,
    './dir/img1.png': __img1png,
  }
  return new URL(modules[`./dir/${name}.png`], import.meta.url).href
}
```

:::

::: warning Does not work with SSR
This pattern does not work if you are using Vite for Server-Side Rendering, because `import.meta.url` has different semantics in browsers vs. Node.js. The server bundle also cannot determine the client host URL ahead of time.
:::

# Backend Integration

:::tip Note
If you want to serve the HTML using a traditional backend (e.g. Rails, Laravel) but use Vite for serving assets, check for existing integrations listed in [Awesome Vite](https://github.com/vitejs/awesome-vite#integrations-with-backends).

If you need a custom integration, you can follow the steps in this guide to configure it manually.
:::

1. In your Vite config, configure the entry and enable build manifest:

   ```js twoslash [vite.config.js]
   import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
   // ---cut---
   export default defineConfig({
     // overwrite default .html entry
     input: '/path/to/main.js',
     server: {
       cors: {
         // the origin you will be accessing via browser
         origin: 'http://my-backend.example.com',
       },
     },
     build: {
       // generate .vite/manifest.json in outDir
       manifest: true,
     },
   })
   ```

   If you haven't disabled the [module preload polyfill](/config/build-options.md#build-polyfillmodulepreload), you also need to import the polyfill in your entry

   ```js
   // add the beginning of your app entry
   import 'vite/modulepreload-polyfill'
   ```

2. For development, inject the following in your server's HTML template (substitute `http://localhost:5173` with the local URL Vite is running at):

   ```html
   <!-- if development -->
   <script type="module" src="http://localhost:5173/@vite/client"></script>
   <script type="module" src="http://localhost:5173/main.js"></script>
   ```

   In order to properly serve assets, you have two options:
   - Make sure the server is configured to proxy static assets requests to the Vite server
   - Set [`server.origin`](/config/server-options.md#server-origin) so that generated asset URLs will be resolved using the back-end server URL instead of a relative path

   This is needed for assets such as images to load properly.

   Note if you are using React with `@vitejs/plugin-react`, you'll also need to add this before the above scripts, since the plugin is not able to modify the HTML you are serving (substitute `http://localhost:5173` with the local URL Vite is running at):

   ```html

     RefreshRuntime.injectIntoGlobalHook(window)
     window.$RefreshReg$ = () => {}
     window.$RefreshSig$ = () => (type) => type
   ```

report.overview: This is the Vite monorepo (`@vitejs/vite-monorepo`) at v8.3.0 — a pnpm workspace shipping three published packages: `vite` (the native-ESM dev server + Rolldown-powered bundler), `create-vite` (the scaffolding CLI), and `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` (SystemJS/Babel downlevel output for old browsers). The `vite` package is the bulk of it: a `cac`-driven CLI over four commands (dev/build/optimize/preview), a `connect` middleware stack that transforms modules on demand and pushes HMR over an authenticated WebSocket, and a Rollup-compatible plugin container that now runs on Rolldown/Oxc rather than Rollup+esbuild. What's distinctive at this commit is the Environment API — dev and build are both fanned out across named environments (`client`, `ssr`, custom) each with its own module graph, plugin container and optimizer — plus an experimental `bundledDev` mode that swaps the per-module transform pipeline for a lazy Rolldown dev bundle served from memory. Correctness is enforced almost entirely by a 83-playground / 109-spec Playwright+Vitest integration suite that runs every fixture in serve, bundled-dev, and build modes.

system_map.summary: Three publishable packages under `packages/`, a 83-directory `playground/` that doubles as the integration test corpus, and a VitePress `docs/` site deployed to Netlify. The `vite` package's runtime splits four ways: `src/node` (server, build, config, plugins — Node only), `src/client` (browser HMR client and error overlay), `src/module-runner` (SSR/runtime module evaluation), and `src/shared` (code compiled into both sides). All bundling — of Vite itself, of user configs, of dep pre-bundles, and of production output — goes through Rolldown; Rollup remains only as a type source and devDependency. There is no database or persistent store; the only on-disk state is the dep-optimizer cache under `cacheDir` and build output under `outDir`.

claims.claim: The published CLI entry is `packages/vite/bin/vite.js`, a thin launcher that enables source maps, installs an `unhandledRejection` trap, parses `-d/--debug`, `-f/--filter` and `--profile` out of `process.argv` *before* importing `../dist/node/cli.js`, and calls `module.enableCompileCache()` with a 10s `flushCompileCache` timer.

`packages/vite/src/node/cli.ts` registers exactly four `cac` commands: the default `[root]` (aliased `serve` and `dev`), `build [root]`, `optimize [root]` (marked deprecated in its own description), and `preview [root]`; each dynamically `import()`s its implementation module so the dev path never loads `build.ts`.

The package's public API surface is `packages/vite/src/node/index.ts`, which re-exports `createServer`, `build`, `createBuilder`, `preview`, `optimizeDeps`, `defineConfig`/`resolveConfig`/`loadConfigFromFile`, `runnerImport`, `fetchModule`, `createServerHotChannel`, `transformWithOxc`, `preprocessCSS`, and `parseAst`/`parseAstAsync` aliased from Rolldown.

`package.json` `exports` publishes four entry points — `.` → `dist/node/index.js`, `./module-runner` → `dist/node/module-runner.js`, `./internal` → `dist/node/internal.js`, and raw `./dist/client/*` — with `./types/internal/*` explicitly nulled to keep internal types unreachable.

Vite builds itself with Rolldown, not Rollup: `rolldown.config.ts` emits separate browser bundles for `src/client/env.ts` → `dist/client/env.mjs`, `src/client/clientEntry.ts` → `dist/client/client.mjs`, and `src/client/bundledDevClient.ts` → `dist/client/bundledDevClient.mjs`, plus a Node ESM bundle with `node/[name].js` entries and `node/chunks/` shared chunks.

The dev server is a `connect()` app, not a framework: `_createServer` builds `middlewares = connect()`, wraps it in `resolveHttpServer`, attaches `createWebSocketServer`, and creates a `chokidar` watcher over root + `config.configFileDependencies` + env files + `publicDir`.

Runtime state is owned per-environment, not globally: `_createServer` iterates `config.environments` calling `environmentOptions.dev.createEnvironment(name, config, { ws })` and `environment.init({ watcher, previousInstance })`, so each of `client`/`ssr`/custom gets its own `DevEnvironment` with its own `moduleGraph` and `pluginContainer`.

The legacy flat `server.moduleGraph` / `server.pluginContainer` / `server.transformRequest` APIs still exist but are getters that call `warnFutureDeprecation(config, 'removeServerModuleGraph')` etc. and delegate to the client environment via a `ModuleGraph` facade in `mixedModuleGraph.ts`.

Production builds go through `createBuilder` → `builder.buildApp()` → per-environment `buildEnvironment()`, which calls `resolveRolldownOptions(environment, chunkMetadataMap)` then `rolldown(...)` and `bundle.write|generate`; `--watch` instead returns a Rolldown `watch()` watcher wired to BUNDLE_START/BUNDLE_END/ERROR events.

The pnpm workspace spans `packages/*`, `playground/**`, nested `packages/**/__tests__/**`, and `docs`, with `overrides: { vite: 'workspace:*' }` so every playground resolves the local build, and patched deps for `sirv@3.0.2`, `chokidar@3.6.0` and `dotenv-expand@13.0.0`.

Build/test commands are all at the root: `pnpm build` (`pnpm -r --filter='./packages/*' run build`), `pnpm test` = `test-unit && test-serve && test-build`, plus `test-serve-bundled` which sets `VITE_TEST_BUNDLED_DEV=1`, and `ci-publish` (`tsx scripts/publishCI.ts`).

Docs are a separate VitePress app (`@vitejs/monorepo-docs`) with a 592-line `docs/.vitepress/config.ts`, deployed by Netlify via `command = "pnpm ci-docs"` publishing `docs/.vitepress/dist`, gated by `scripts/docs-check.sh` as the ignore predicate.

External integrations are optional peer deps resolved lazily: `sass`/`sass-embedded`/`less`/`stylus`/`sugarss` for CSS, `terser` for minification, `jiti`/`tsx` for config loading, and `@vitejs/devtools` (loaded via `await import('@vitejs/devtools/integration')` inside `builder.runDevTools()`).

The repo now depends on hosted build-cache infrastructure: `@voidzero-dev/vite-task-client` supplies `disableCache()` (called first thing in `_createServer` because dev output can't be replayed) and `getEnv('NODE_ENV')`/`getEnvs` used during config and env resolution.

feature_catalog.summary: Vite's user-facing surface is four CLI commands, a programmatic JS API, a Rollup-superset plugin hook system, and a browser-side HMR runtime with an error overlay. Around that sit optional subsystems: dependency pre-bundling, CSS preprocessing and modules, worker/WASM/asset handling, `import.meta.glob`, SSR module running, and the legacy-browser plugin. `create-vite` is an independent interactive scaffolder with eleven framework families. The most recently added features are the multi-environment builder (`--app` / `builder: {}`), console forwarding from browser to terminal, and `--experimentalBundle` bundled dev.

claims.claim: `vite dev` accepts `--host`, `--port`, `--open [path]`, `--cors`, `--strictPort`, `--force` (bust the optimizer cache) and `--experimentalBundle`, then prints URLs and installs CLI shortcuts, adding a `p` shortcut to toggle the CPU profiler when launched under `--profile`.

`vite build` exposes `--target`, `--outDir`, `--assetsDir`, `--assetsInlineLimit`, `--ssr [entry]`, `--sourcemap [inline|hidden]`, `--minify [oxc|terser|esbuild]` (default `oxc`), `--manifest`, `--ssrManifest`, `--emptyOutDir`, `-w/--watch`, and `--app` which is sugar for `builder: {}`.
Interactive terminal shortcuts during dev are `r` restart server, `u` show server url, `o` open in browser, `c` clear console, `q` quit; preview mode registers only `o` and `q`.

The dev server exposes built-in HTTP endpoints beyond module serving: `/__open-in-editor` (via `launch-editor-middleware`), a `viteHMRPingMiddleware` answering `accept: text/x-vite-ping` with 204, and `/@fs/` raw filesystem serving guarded by the allow-list.

A dev proxy is available via `server.proxy`, backed by `http-proxy-3`, supporting `rewrite`, `configure`, webpack-dev-server-style `bypass`, WebSocket proxying, and `rewriteWsOrigin` to rewrite the Origin header on WS upgrades.

The browser client ships an error overlay implemented as the custom element `vite-error-overlay` (`class ErrorOverlay extends HTMLElement`), gated by the injected `__HMR_ENABLE_OVERLAY__` define and creatable/clearable from `handleMessage`.

Dependency pre-bundling is a full subsystem: `scanImports` computes entries and runs a Rolldown scanner, `runOptimizeDeps` writes a `_metadata.json` cache under `getDepsCacheDir(environment)`, and `loadCachedDepOptimizationMetadata` / `cleanupDepsCacheStaleDirs` manage reuse and GC across runs.

The built-in plugin pipeline provides asset handling, CSS (`cssPlugin`/`cssPostPlugin`/`cssAnalysisPlugin`), HTML (`htmlInlineProxyPlugin`/`buildHtmlPlugin`), web workers (`webWorkerPlugin`, `workerImportMetaUrlPlugin`), WASM (`wasmHelperPlugin`), `define`, `import.meta.glob` (`importGlobPlugin`), dynamic-import variables, and module-preload polyfill.

Browser console forwarding to the terminal is opt-in via `server.forwardConsole.enabled`, which conditionally inserts `forwardConsolePlugin({ environments: ['client'] })` into the pipeline and is picked up client-side through the `__SERVER_FORWARD_CONSOLE__` define.

SSR is served by `fetchModule(environment, url, importer)`, which short-circuits `data:` URLs and Node builtins to `{externalize, type:'builtin'}`, external URLs to `type:'network'`, and otherwise resolves bare specifiers through `tryNodeResolve` with `externalConditions`.

`vite/module-runner` is a separately published runtime: `class ModuleRunner` with `evaluatedModules`, a pluggable `transport` that `invoke('fetchModule', ...)`s the server, optional HMR via `createHMRHandlerForRunner`, and `cachedRequest`/`directRequest` for circular-dependency-aware evaluation.

`create-vite` v9.2.1 is an interactive prompt-driven scaffolder over a `FRAMEWORKS` table covering vanilla, vue, react, preact, lit, svelte, solid and qwik, each with TS/JS variants plus links to external starters (Nuxt, Vike, Official Vue Starter), materialised from the sibling `template-*` directories.

`@vitejs/plugin-legacy` v8.2.3 returns a plugin array (`legacyConfigPlugin`, `legacyGenerateBundlePlugin`, `legacyPostPlugin`) that runs `detectPolyfills`, transforms modern chunks to SystemJS via `@babel/plugin-transform-modules-systemjs`, injects `systemjs/dist/s.min.js`, and emits a `systemjs-importmap` script tag.

Experimental full-bundle dev mode (`--experimentalBundle` → `config.experimental.bundledDev`) replaces the transform/static middlewares with `triggerLazyBundlingMiddleware` + `memoryFilesMiddleware` and is driven by the `BundledDev` class holding a `MemoryFiles` map and a Rolldown dev engine started with `experimental.devMode = { lazy: true }`.

data_flow.summary: Three input boundaries feed the system: the config file (loaded by bundling, runner-import, or native import), `.env` files filtered by prefix, and HTTP/WS requests from the browser. Config flows into a single frozen `ResolvedConfig` that fans out into per-environment configs; each `DevEnvironment` then owns a `EnvironmentModuleGraph` as the authoritative in-memory state. A request's data path is URL → plugin container `resolveId`→`load`→`transform` → optional `ssrTransform` → cached `TransformResult` (code + map + etag + deps) stored on the module node and written back out through `send()`. The reverse direction — file change → HMR payload → WebSocket → browser — is the only push channel. In build mode the same plugin container is driven by Rolldown instead of by HTTP requests, and the terminal output boundary is `outDir` plus optional `manifest.json`/`ssr-manifest.json`.

claims.claim: Config entry: `resolveConfig` merges inline config over the file config from `loadConfigFromFile`, then re-derives `mode`, filters plugins by `apply`, runs `config` hooks via `runConfigHook`, and force-injects `client` (and usually `ssr`) into `config.environments` before per-environment resolution.

`loadConfigFromFile` picks one of three loaders selected by `--configLoader`: `bundleAndLoadConfigFile` (default — Rolldown-bundles the config then evaluates it), `runnerImportConfigFile` (uses Vite's own module runner), or `nativeImportConfigFile` (raw `import()` of a `file://` URL with a `?t=` cache-buster, or `fresh-import`).

Env vars enter through `loadEnv(mode, envDir, prefixes = 'VITE_')`, which reads `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.<mode>`, `.env.<mode>.local` (accepting FIFOs so 1Password-style pipes work), parses with `node:util` `parseEnv`, then expands with `dotenv-expand` against a *copy* of `process.env` so expansion doesn't mutate the global.

`transformRequest(environment, url, options)` dedupes concurrent work through `environment._pendingRequests` keyed by timestamp-stripped URL, and records a `monotonicDateNow()` timestamp up front so a transform that races an invalidation is discarded rather than cached stale.

Inside `loadAndTransform` the order is `pluginContainer.load(id)` → fall back to reading from disk → `pluginContainer.transform(code, id, ...)` → `ssrTransform(code, normalizedMap, url, originalCode, ...)` when the environment needs module-runner output.

The transform result carries `{ code, map, ssr?, etag?, deps?, dynamicDeps? }`; the etag is what `cachedTransformMiddleware` matches against `if-none-match` via `moduleGraph.getModuleByEtag` to short-circuit with a 304.

`importAnalysisPlugin` is the rewrite stage that converts every import specifier to a server-resolvable URL via its internal `normalizeUrl`, records importer/imported edges on the module graph, and computes `isSelfAccepting` from `import.meta.hot.accept` calls — the data the HMR propagation algorithm later consumes.

HMR output is one of two payload shapes computed in `updateModules`: a `{type:'full-reload', triggeredBy, path}` message, or a `{type:'update', updates:[...]}` array whose entries carry `path`, `acceptedPath`, `explicitImportRequired`, `isWithinCircularImport` and `firstInvalidatedBy`.

Client-side the payload arrives over a `normalizeModuleRunnerTransport`-wrapped WebSocket opened to `${protocol}://${socketHost}?token=${wsToken}` with subprotocol `vite-hmr`, and is dispatched by `handleMessage` into `hmrClient.queueUpdate(update)`.

Static assets bypass the transform pipeline entirely: `servePublicMiddleware` is registered *before* `transformMiddleware` specifically so `publicDir` files are served as-is, and `serveRawFsMiddleware` handles `/@fs/`-prefixed absolute paths by slicing `FS_PREFIX` off the pathname.

In bundled-dev mode the data path inverts: Rolldown produces output files that `BundledDev` stores as lazily-evaluated entries in `MemoryFiles` (including `BUNDLED_DEV_CLIENT_FILENAME`), and `memoryFilesMiddleware` serves from that map instead of from the module graph.

Build-mode data flow is fanned out by environment: `createBuilder` re-runs `resolveConfigToBuild` once per environment name (unless `configBuilder.sharedConfigBuild`) with a `patchPlugins` pass that swaps in shared plugin instances for those marked `sharedDuringBuild`.

Module-runner data flow closes the loop server→runtime: `ModuleRunner.directRequest` calls `this.transport.invoke('fetchModule', [...])`, the server answers from `fetchModule`, and the result is evaluated and cached in `EvaluatedModules` keyed by both id and url.

The `ResolvedConfig` object is also the carrier for two derived security primitives computed once at resolve time: `webSocketToken` (72 random bits, base64url) and `fsDenyGlob` (a `picomatch` matcher built from `server.fs.deny` with `nocase` and `dot` enabled).

behavior_traces.summary: Four flows are worth tracing: dev-server startup, a module request, a file-change HMR round trip, and a production build. Startup is notable for deferring `buildStart` and optimizer init until the HTTP `listen` call is intercepted. The module request path is a long but linear middleware chain. HMR distinguishes config/env changes (full server restart) from module changes (graph propagation). The build path is a per-environment loop over Rolldown.

claims.claim: Dev startup: `bin/vite.js` → `dist/node/cli.js` → the default cac action → `createServer()` → `_createServer` → `disableCache()` → `resolveConfig(inlineConfig,'serve')` → `resolveHttpServer` → `createWebSocketServer` → chokidar watcher → per-environment `createEnvironment`/`init` → middleware registration → `server.listen()`.

Startup defers expensive work by monkey-patching the HTTP server: `httpServer.listen` is replaced with a wrapper that awaits `initServer(true)` first and re-emits any error as an `'error'` event, so `buildStart` and `environment.listen(server)` run exactly once before the socket binds.
In middleware mode there is no HTTP server at all — `httpServer` is `null`, `resolveHttpServer` is skipped, and `initServer(false)` is awaited inline at the end of `_createServer`.

The middleware chain is registered in a fixed order: `timeMiddleware` (only when `process.env.DEBUG`) → `rejectInvalidRequestMiddleware` → `corsMiddleware` → `hostValidationMiddleware` → user `configureServer` hooks → `cachedTransformMiddleware` → `proxyMiddleware` → `baseMiddleware` → `/__open-in-editor` → HMR ping → `servePublicMiddleware` → `transformMiddleware` → `serveRawFsMiddleware` → `serveStaticMiddleware` → `htmlFallbackMiddleware` → post hooks → `indexHtmlMiddleware` → `notFoundMiddleware` → `errorMiddleware`.

`configureServer` hooks run in two phases around the internal middlewares: the hook's synchronous body runs before `cachedTransformMiddleware` is added, while any function it *returns* is pushed to `postHooks` and invoked after the static/HTML-fallback middlewares but before `indexHtmlMiddleware`, which is what lets user middleware pre-empt `index.html`.

A module request runs `transformMiddleware` → `environment.transformRequest(url)` → `transformRequest` (pending-request dedupe) → `doTransform` (`pluginContainer.resolveId`) → `loadAndTransform` (`pluginContainer.load`, then `pluginContainer.transform`) → optional `ssrTransform` → `send()` with the etag.

`EnvironmentPluginContainer.resolveId` lazily triggers `this.buildStart()` and awaits `_buildStartPromise` on the first resolution, so for non-client environments the `buildStart` hook fires on first request rather than at server boot.

File change → `watcher.on('change')` → `onFileChange` → `handleHMRUpdate(type, file, server)`, which first checks whether the file is `config.configFile`, a member of `config.configFileDependencies`, or an env file for the current mode — any of those triggers `restartServerWithUrls(server)` instead of an HMR update.

`handleHMRUpdate` snapshots `server.environments` and defines `isStale()` comparing identity, because a `hotUpdate`/`handleHotUpdate` plugin hook may restart the server mid-transaction and invalidate the whole HMR pass.

Edits to Vite's own client directory can't be hot-updated: if the changed file starts with `normalizedClientDir`, every environment immediately gets `hot.send({ type:'full-reload', path:'*' })` and the function returns.

`updateModules` runs `propagateUpdate(mod, traversedModules, boundaries)` per changed module, invalidates via `moduleGraph.invalidateModule`, and escalates to full reload on any dead end, on an empty `modules` array, on `circular import invalidate`, or when a client-environment `.html` file changes and none of its modules are of type `js`.

Production build: `cli.ts` build action → `createBuilder(inlineConfig, null)` → `builder.buildApp()` → sorted `buildApp` plugin hooks with `configBuilder.buildApp(builder)` interleaved before `order:'post'` hooks → fallback loop calling `builder.build(environment)` for any environment still `!isBuilt` → `buildEnvironment` → `rolldown()` → `bundle.write()` → `builder.runDevTools()`.

Server shutdown runs `closeServer(reason)` which `Promise.allSettled`s watcher close, ws close, every `environment.close()`, `closeHttpServer()` and `_ssrCompatModuleRunner?.close()`, and only *afterwards* invokes the sorted `closeServer` plugin hooks with `{ reason }`.

Browser reconnection is handled separately from HMR: `client.ts` opens a second WebSocket with the `vite-ping` subprotocol, which the server's `shouldHandle` allows from any origin without a token and which `handleUpgrade` closes immediately with code 1000 so the pinging client is never added to `wss.clients`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is Vitest-only, split into two configs. `vitest.config.ts` collects 68 unit specs from `**/__tests__/**/*.spec.[tj]s` inside `packages/`, running with `isolate: false` and a 20s timeout. `vitest.config.e2e.ts` collects 109 integration specs from `playground/**`, driving a real Playwright Chromium browser against real Vite servers. The integration suite is the primary correctness net and runs three times in CI — serve, bundled-dev, and build — across Node 20/22/24/26 on Ubuntu plus macOS and Windows. The weakest spot is that unit coverage of the largest files is thin relative to their size: `css.ts` (3685 lines) and `hmr.ts` (1193 lines) have no dedicated unit spec, and are covered only indirectly through playground fixtures.

claims.claim: Unit tests use `vitest.config.ts` with `include: ['**/__tests__/**/*.spec.[tj]s']`, explicitly excluding `./playground/**` and `./playground-temp/**`, `testTimeout: 20000`, `isolate: false`, and an alias mapping `vite/module-runner` to the TypeScript source rather than `dist`.

There are 68 unit spec files under `packages/**/__tests__/`, concentrated in `packages/vite/src/node/__tests__/` (config, build, dev, env, html, http, resolve, scan, utils, oxc, packages, shortcuts, external, environment, filterRegex, assetSource) plus `plugins/`, `optimizer/` and `utils/` subdirectories.

Integration tests use `vitest.config.e2e.ts` with `include: ['./playground/**/*.spec.[tj]s']`, `globalSetup: playground/vitestGlobalSetup.ts`, `setupFiles: playground/vitestSetup.ts`, `reporters: 'dot'`, and a timeout of 50s on CI / 30s locally (Infinity under `PWDEBUG`).

`vitestGlobalSetup.ts` launches a shared `chromium.launchServer()` (headed when `VITE_DEBUG_SERVE` is set, `--no-sandbox` on CI), shares the endpoint via `project.provide('wsEndpoint', ...)`, then copies only the playground directories actually referenced by the selected test files into `playground-temp/`.

`vitestSetup.ts` exposes the per-test harness — `page`, `viteTestUrl`, `browserLogs`, `browserErrors`, `serverLogs`, and mode flags `isBuild`/`isServe`/`isBundledDev`/`isBundled` — aliased in tests as `~utils`.

The same 109 playground specs are executed under three different modes selected by env vars: default serve, `VITE_TEST_BUNDLED_DEV=1` (`test-serve-bundled`), and `VITE_TEST_BUILD=1` (`test-build`), with `NODE_ENV` set to `production` only in the build run.

Known gaps in bundled-dev mode are tracked as an explicit 22-entry `bundledDevExclude` array in `vitest.config.e2e.ts` — including `fs-serve`, `csp`, `hmr-ssr`, `optimize-deps`, `tailwind` and all four `worker` variants — with the convention that partial failures use `test.skipIf(isBundledDev)` instead of listing the file.

CI runs the full matrix Node 20/22/24/26 on ubuntu-latest plus macos-latest@24 and windows-latest@24.15.0 (pinned to work around nodejs/node#63638), with `fail-fast: false` and a 20-minute timeout per job.

The CI `test` job runs all four suites sequentially — `test-unit`, `test-serve`, `test-serve-bundled`, `test-build` — after a `pnpm run build`, and a separate `lint` job runs eslint, `pnpm format && git diff --exit-code`, `pnpm typecheck`, and `pnpm test-docs`.

CI skips the whole test matrix when only docs, `.github/**` (excluding `ci.yml`), `packages/create-vite/template**`, or `**.md` changed, via a `changed` job using `tj-actions/changed-files` with `only_changed`.
Flakiness is managed with environment knobs rather than retries in test code: `VITEST_SEGFAULT_RETRY: 3` and `NODE_OPTIONS: --max-old-space-size=6144` are set globally in the workflow env block.

A scheduled Semgrep scan (`--config auto`, weekly on Tuesdays) uploads SARIF to GitHub code scanning, but explicitly excludes `playground` and `__tests__` and disables the `detect-non-literal-regexp` rule — so dynamic regex construction in source is not flagged.

Type-level tests exist as a separate mechanism: `src/node/__tests_dts__` and `src/module-runner/__tests_dts__` are compiled by the package `typecheck` script (`tsc -p src/node/__tests_dts__`), using `@type-challenges/utils`.

Type output is separately validated after bundling: `build-types` runs `rolldown.dts.config.ts` then `tsc --project tsconfig.check.json`, and CONTRIBUTING documents `pnpm run build-types-check` as the guard against d.ts leaking devDependency types.

risk_map.summary: Vite's security model rests on four independent guards — the `server.fs` allow/deny list, WebSocket token authentication, host validation, and CORS origin restriction — and a bypass in any one of them exposes the developer's filesystem or dev server to a hostile web page. The code shows scar tissue from past CVEs: Windows 8.3 short-name detection, NTFS ADS colon rejection, `#`-in-URL rejection, and trailing-slash normalisation are all defensive patches with explanatory comments. Beyond security, the main structural risks are the very large monolithic modules (`css.ts` at 3685 lines, `config.ts` at 2961), the two-implementation split between classic dev and `bundledDev`, and a large surface of deprecated-but-live compatibility shims.

claims.claim: `isFileLoadingAllowed` is the single chokepoint for filesystem access and carries three separate bypass mitigations: Windows 8.3 short-name paths (`PROGRA~1`, matched by `windowsShortNameSegmentRE`) are rejected outright, any `:` outside a drive letter is rejected as a possible NTFS alternate data stream, and trailing slashes are stripped before the deny check because `fs.readFile('/foo.png/')` resolves to `/foo.png`.

`server.fs.deny` defaults to only six patterns — `.env`, `.env.*`, `*.{crt,pem,key,p12,pfx,cer,der}`, `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, `**/.git/**` — so any other secret-bearing file inside an allowed root (e.g. `credentials.json`, `.aws/`, `id_rsa` without extension) is servable when `fs.strict` passes.

`config.safeModulePaths` is an escape hatch checked *before* the `fs.allow` list in `isFileLoadingAllowed`, and it is populated at runtime by `DevEnvironment._registerInputsAsSafeModules()` — meaning build inputs silently widen the serving allow-list.

`rejectInvalidRequestMiddleware` exists specifically because Node accepts `#` in request targets while the `server.fs.deny` checks assume it is absent — a 400 is returned for any URL containing `#`, and this middleware is the first in the chain.

WebSocket auth uses a per-process 72-bit token compared with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, but the token travels as a URL query parameter (`?token=...`), which the comment acknowledges may land in server/middleware logs.
`config.legacy.skipWebSocketTokenCheck` is a live opt-out that disables token validation entirely inside `shouldHandle`, re-opening cross-site WebSocket hijacking for anyone who sets it.

Host validation is skipped whenever `server.https` is configured (`if (allowedHosts !== true && !serverConfig.https)`), on the reasoning that HTTPS is not DNS-rebinding-vulnerable — so a misissued or self-signed HTTPS dev setup loses that guard.

The WS upgrade path allows *any* non-browser client without a token: `shouldHandle` returns `true` when `req.headers.origin` is absent, with an inline comment justifying it for backward compat — meaning any local process that can open a socket can join the HMR channel.

Shell-out surface exists in the dev server itself: `server/index.ts` imports `execSync` from `node:child_process`, and `openBrowser.ts` spawns a browser process honouring the `BROWSER`/`BROWSER_ARGS` environment variables which `loadEnv` will populate from a project's `.env` file.

Config loading executes arbitrary project code by design through three paths (`bundleAndLoadConfigFile`, `runnerImportConfigFile`, `nativeImportConfigFile`), and `bundleConfigFile`/`loadConfigFromBundledFile` evaluate the bundled result — so opening an untrusted repo and running `vite` is code execution.

Blast-radius hotspots by size: `plugins/css.ts` (3685 lines), `config.ts` (2961), `utils.ts` (2022), `build.ts` (1986), `plugins/html.ts` (1753), `server/index.ts` (1496), `server/pluginContainer.ts` (1332) — none of which has a same-named unit spec except `config.spec.ts`, `build.spec.ts` and `html.spec.ts`.

The dev server now has two divergent implementations gated on one boolean: `config.experimental.bundledDev` swaps the entire serving strategy, skips `cachedTransformMiddleware`, skips `buildStart` at init, and short-circuits `handleHMRUpdate` with a `// TODO: support handleHotUpdate / hotUpdate` early return — so plugin HMR hooks silently do nothing in that mode.

A large deprecated-but-live compatibility layer runs on every access: `server.hot`, `server.pluginContainer`, `server.moduleGraph`, `server.transformRequest`, `server.warmupRequest`, `server.ssrLoadModule`, `server.ssrFixStacktrace`, `server.ssrRewriteStacktrace` and `server.reloadModule` all route through `warnFutureDeprecation` and a `ModuleGraph` bridging facade.

`vite optimize` is documented-dead in its own help string ('deprecated, the pre-bundle process runs automatically and does not need to be called') yet still resolves a full config and invokes `optimizeDeps(config, options.force, true)`.

The preview server reuses `hostValidationMiddleware(allowedHosts, true)` and `sirv(distDir, ...)` but has a much shorter middleware chain than the dev server and no `fs.allow` equivalent, since it serves a fixed `distDir` root.

`server.proxy`'s `rewriteWsOrigin` deliberately rewrites the browser-supplied `Origin` header on WebSocket upgrades, with an inline warning path when headers are already sent — a knob that defeats the target server's own origin checks if enabled carelessly.

extension_points.summary: Vite's primary extension mechanism is the plugin object — a superset of Rolldown/Rollup's, adding `config`, `configEnvironment`, `configureServer`, `configurePreviewServer`, `transformIndexHtml`, `hotUpdate`, `buildApp`, and the environment-scoping fields `applyToEnvironment`/`sharedDuringBuild`. The ordered array returned by `resolvePlugins` is the canonical insertion-point table: user `pre`, `normal` and `post` plugins are spliced at three fixed positions between internal plugins. Beyond plugins, the extension surface includes the environment factory (`dev.createEnvironment`/`build.createEnvironment`), the hot-channel/transport abstraction, the CLI shortcut table, and the `create-vite` template directory convention.

claims.claim: `resolvePlugins(config, prePlugins, normalPlugins, postPlugins)` is the ordering contract: user `pre` plugins land after the alias plugins, `normal` plugins after asset/CSS/worker handling but before `definePlugin`, and `post` plugins after the glob/dynamic-import plugins — with `clientInjectionsPlugin`, `cssAnalysisPlugin` and `importAnalysisPlugin` always last.

`getSortedPluginsByHook(hookName, plugins)` implements the per-hook `order: 'pre' | 'post'` sorting with three running indices, and `createPluginHookUtils` memoises the result per hook name into `getSortedPlugins`/`getSortedPluginHooks` on the resolved config.

`applyToEnvironment(environment)` lets a plugin opt in/out per environment or return a *replacement* plugin — as the built-in alias plugin does, swapping itself for Rolldown's native `nativeAliasPlugin` when `environment.config.isBundled` and no custom resolver is present.
`perEnvironmentPlugin(name, applyToEnvironment)` is the public helper for building environment-scoped plugins, exported from the package root alongside `perEnvironmentState`.

`buildApp` is the multi-environment build orchestration hook: `builder.buildApp()` walks `config.getSortedPlugins('buildApp')` and interleaves `configBuilder.buildApp(builder)` just before the first `order: 'post'` hook, letting frameworks control environment build order and interdependencies.

`hotUpdate` is the environment-aware replacement for `handleHotUpdate`: `getSortedHotUpdatePlugins(environment)` selects the plugins and each hook receives a `HotUpdateOptions` with `{type, file, timestamp, read, server, modules}` and may return a filtered module list.

Environments are created through configurable factories — `environmentOptions.dev.createEnvironment(name, config, { ws })` at server start and `config.build.createEnvironment(name, config)` in `createBuilder.setupEnvironment` — with `defaultCreateDevEnvironment`/`defaultCreateClientDevEnvironment` as the built-in defaults.

The HMR transport is pluggable on both ends: server-side via `normalizeHotChannel` and `createServerHotChannel()` (exported publicly), client/runtime-side via `normalizeModuleRunnerTransport` and `createWebSocketModuleRunnerTransport` in `src/shared/moduleRunnerTransport.ts`.

`bindCLIShortcuts({ print, customShortcuts })` accepts an array of `CLIShortcut<Server>` objects (`{ key, description, action }`) merged with the built-in table — the mechanism the CLI itself uses to add the `p` profiler toggle.

Plugin hook filtering is an extension point with its own registry: `getCachedFilterForPlugin(plugin, hookName)` builds and WeakMap-caches `createIdFilter` / `createFilterForTransform` matchers from a hook's `filter: { id, code, moduleType }` object.

`createIdResolver(config, options)` is exported as the supported way for plugins to reuse Vite's resolver, and `config.createResolver(options)` wraps it with per-environment `PartialEnvironment` instances for client and ssr.

`create-vite` extends purely by directory convention — each entry in the `FRAMEWORKS` variants table maps to a sibling `template-<name>` directory (`template-react-ts`, `template-svelte`, `template-qwik-ts`, …), so adding a template means adding a directory plus a table entry.

The dev-server middleware chain is extensible only through `configureServer` (pre and post phases) and `configurePreviewServer`; there is no separate middleware registry, so ordering is controlled by which phase a plugin uses.

DevTools integration is a first-class optional extension: `loadDevToolsIntegrationPlugins(config, command, devtoolsOptions)` injects plugins during `resolveConfig`, and `resolveDevToolsConfig` / `isDevToolsOptionEnabled` gate it behind the optional `@vitejs/devtools` peer dependency.

agent_handoff.summary: This is a high-traffic OSS monorepo with strict conventions: pnpm only (enforced by `only-allow` in `preinstall`), oxfmt for formatting, eslint for `packages/*/{src,types}/**/*.ts`, and a `simple-git-hooks` pre-commit running lint-staged. Almost nothing can be verified without first running `pnpm build`, since the playground tests execute the built `dist/node/cli.js`. Read the CLI, server bootstrap, config resolver, and plugin pipeline before touching anything; treat the security guards and the deprecation shims as append-only unless the change is deliberate. The most common trap is editing `packages/vite/src/node` and testing without rebuilding, or adding a runtime dependency to the wrong section of `package.json`.

claims.claim: Read first, in order: `packages/vite/src/node/cli.ts` (command surface), `packages/vite/src/node/server/index.ts` (`_createServer` + middleware order), `packages/vite/src/node/config.ts` (`resolveConfig`, `loadConfigFromFile`), `packages/vite/src/node/plugins/index.ts` (`resolvePlugins` ordering) and `packages/vite/src/node/build.ts` (`createBuilder`/`buildEnvironment`).

Setup is `pnpm i` then `pnpm run build` at the repo root; while developing Vite itself, run `pnpm run dev` inside `packages/vite` for a watching Rolldown rebuild (`premove dist && pnpm build-bundle -w`).
pnpm is mandatory — root `preinstall` runs `npx only-allow pnpm` and `packageManager` pins `pnpm@12.4.2`; npm/yarn installs will be rejected.

Verification commands: `pnpm test-unit` (fast, no browser), `pnpm test-serve [match]` / `pnpm test-build [match]` for targeted playground runs, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm format` (oxfmt), and `pnpm typecheck` (root `tsc -p scripts` plus every package's own typecheck).

Playground test matching is per-substring and only works on `test-serve`/`test-build`, not on `pnpm test` — e.g. `pnpm run test-serve assets` runs both `playground/assets` and `playground/assets-sanitize`.

Trap: playground tests run against a real `vite` binary resolved through `viteBinPath` in `vitestSetup.ts`, so source edits in `packages/vite/src` are invisible to integration tests until `pnpm build` (or a running `pnpm dev` watcher) regenerates `dist`.

Trap: the e2e global setup copies playgrounds into `playground-temp/` and only copies the directories matched by the selected spec files — a new fixture directory that no spec references will not be copied, and `VITE_PRESERVE_BUILD_ARTIFACTS=1` (via `pnpm debug-build`) is needed to inspect the output.

Dependency placement is a reviewed decision: `packages/vite/package.json` carries a literal `"//": "READ CONTRIBUTING.md to understand what to put under deps vs. devDeps!"` marker, and CONTRIBUTING has sections on `require()` usage, adding dependencies, and ensuring type support.

Formatting and linting are enforced on commit: `simple-git-hooks` pre-commit runs `lint-staged --concurrent false`, which applies `oxfmt` to all files and eslint `--fix` to `packages/*/{src,types}/**/*.ts`, `packages/**/*.d.ts` and `playground/**/__tests__/**/*.ts`.

Safe edit boundary: anything under `playground/` is fixture + spec code, not shipped code — only `packages/vite`, `packages/create-vite` and `packages/plugin-legacy` are published, and CI skips tests entirely for `packages/create-vite/template**` changes.

Do not relax the filesystem guards casually: `isFileLoadingAllowed`, `looksLikeWindowsShortNamePath`, the NTFS-colon check and `rejectInvalidRequestMiddleware` each carry comments identifying a specific bypass class they exist to block.

When adding a server-facing API, mirror the environment convention: put state on `DevEnvironment` (which owns `moduleGraph`, `pluginContainer`, `_pendingRequests`, `transformRequest`, `warmupRequest`, `waitForRequestsIdle`) and expose any flat `server.*` alias only through `warnFutureDeprecation`.

Debug logging convention: use `createDebugger('vite:<area>')` (e.g. `vite:load`, `vite:transform`, `vite:cache`, `vite:env`, `vite:hmr`) and keep middleware functions *named*, since the names surface under `DEBUG=connect:dispatcher` — several files carry that exact comment.

Releases are automated and should not be hand-driven: `publish.yml` runs `scripts/detect-release.ts` against the latest commit subject on pushes to `main`/`v[0-9]*`, and `pnpm ci-publish` invokes `scripts/publishCI.ts`; `prepare-release.yml` and `scripts/prepare-release.ts` handle version bumps.
The repo has an explicit AI Policy section in CONTRIBUTING.md alongside the Pull Request Guidelines and issue-triaging workflow — read it before opening a PR from an agent-assisted change.
